subject: Communications
learning_objective: Identify items that must be read back
question_text: Which item from ATC must always be read back?
explanation: SERA.8015(e)(1): the items that must always be read back include ATC route clearances; runway entry, landing, take-off, hold-short, crossing, taxi and backtrack clearances; and the runway in use, altimeter settings, SSR codes, new frequencies, level, heading and speed instructions and transition levels.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Wind is not on the SERA list of items that must always be read back.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Traffic information is acknowledged, not necessarily read back.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Temperature is not on the list of mandatory read-back items.

syllabus_version: EASA Part-FCL LAPL/PPL theoretical knowledge syllabus (current EAR edition; LO numbering not verified this session)
subject: Communications
learning_objective: Identify runway clearances that must be read back
question_text: ATC instructs a pilot to hold short of the runway. What must the pilot do?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Read back the hold-short instruction with the aircraft call sign

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reply with the call sign only

choices.label: D
choices.text: Acknowledge by flashing the landing light

explanation: SERA.8015(e)(1)(ii) requires read-back of clearances and instructions to enter, land on, take off from, hold short of, cross, taxi on and backtrack on any runway. SERA.14055(c)(2) requires the call sign to be added when reading back clearances.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Hold-short instructions must be read back; ROGER alone is not enough.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Runway instructions must be read back in full.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Read-back is by voice on the frequency.

regulation_reference: SERA.8015(e)(1)(ii); SERA.14055(c)(2) - EASA Easy Access Rules for Standardised European Rules of the Air (SERA), Regulation (EU) No 923/2012 consolidated (EAR SERA, revision August 2025)

subject: Communications
question_text: When may a pilot start using the abbreviated form of the aircraft's call sign?

choices.label: A
choices.text: As soon as the pilot has made the first call

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only after the aeronautical station has addressed the aircraft by its abbreviated call sign

choices.label: D
choices.text: Never; full call signs are always required

explanation: SERA.14055(c)(1): abbreviated call signs may be used only after satisfactory communication has been established and no confusion is likely. An aircraft uses its abbreviated call sign only after the aeronautical station has addressed it that way.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: The ground station must abbreviate first.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Abbreviation depends on the ground station having used it, not on frequency loading.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Abbreviated call signs are allowed once satisfactory communication is established and the station has used them.

incorrect_answer_explanations.D: ATIS is a broadcast service and cannot respond.

subject: Communications
learning_objective: Apply the VFR radio failure procedure
question_text: A VFR flight suffers a radio communication failure and cannot re-establish contact. What should the pilot do?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Set 7700 and continue to the planned destination in any weather

choices.label: B
choices.text: Climb into cloud to improve radio reception

choices.label: C
choices.text: Land immediately in the nearest field

choices.label: D
choices.text: Set 7600, continue in VMC, land at the nearest suitable aerodrome and report arrival to ATS

explanation: SERA.14083(c)(2)-(3): set transponder code 7600. A VFR flight continues in VMC, lands at the nearest suitable aerodrome, and reports its arrival by the quickest means to the appropriate ATS unit.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: A VFR flight must stay in VMC.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: The procedure is to land at the nearest suitable aerodrome.
